Description: The only Dead Sea Scroll written on metal: three copper sheets (about 99% copper with about 1% tin) riveted end to end, about 2.4 metres by 28 centimetres, with letters punched into the metal in a Hebrew dialect close to Mishnaic Hebrew. It was found on 14 March 1952 at the back of Qumran Cave 3 by Henri de Contenson's team, in two oxidized rolls, and was cut into 23 strips at Manchester in 1955–56 because corrosion made unrolling impossible. It is not a religious text but a list of about 64 treasure caches — gold, silver and vessels — each with place, direction and depth directions, and it is now at the Jordan Museum, Amman.
Interpretations: The Copper Scroll illuminates the world of hidden wealth, revolt and temple treasure in first-century Judea, and it is dated by many scholars to the First Jewish Revolt period (about 66–70 AD). Whether its treasure was real Temple treasure, the community's own wealth, or a legendary list is unresolved, and no cache has ever been conclusively identified from its directions, so it must not be treated as a working treasure map.
BiblicalSignificance: It is a unique material witness to the turmoil of first-century Judea, when temple wealth and hiding valuables from Rome were urgent realities behind the world of the New Testament.
ArtifactDate: c. 50–100 AD (many scholars: First Jewish Revolt period, c. 66–70 AD)
